Project concept

AI workflows for DevOps

From an alert to
verified recovery.

Build an agent that investigates a Kubernetes incident, makes a case for a fix, and checks whether it actually worked.

The operational loop is the project: observe, reason, act with approval, then measure the result.

Incident lifecycleOne agent. A bounded workflow.
  1. 01Notice the failureAn alert carries scope and symptoms.
  2. 02Follow the evidenceQuery, form a hypothesis, query again.
  3. 03Propose a changeA reviewable fix with a recovery plan.
  4. 04Verify the outcomeObserve service health after deployment.
Uncertain diagnosis or failed recovery? Escalate.

Where the AI earns its place
The agent chooses the next question.
A script follows a fixed path. This workflow adapts to the evidence within a controlled set of tools.
Reasoning and investigation
  • Choose whether to inspect events, logs, metrics, or a recent deployment.
  • Compare plausible causes and look for evidence that disproves them.
  • Revise the diagnosis when observations contradict it.
  • Explain what is known, what is missing, and why a fix fits.
Deterministic execution
  • Validate tool arguments, namespace scope, and output size.
  • Enforce permissions, timeouts, and a tool-call budget.
  • Require approval before deploying a proposed change.
  • Run defined health checks and preserve an audit trail.
Start with one agent moving through explicit states. Add specialist agents only when evaluations show that they improve the outcome.


    
System architecture
A small lab. A complete operational loop.
The agent reasons over observations. Git and deployment controls govern changes to the application.

Proposed MVP stack One kind cluster, a small HTTP API, PostgreSQL, Prometheus + Alertmanager, GitHub, Argo CD, and a Python agent service with typed tool wrappers.
State and continuity Persist an incident ID, evidence references, tool calls, approval status, and verification results in SQLite. Resume after approval instead of starting a second investigation.

    


    
Operational boundaries
Give the agent a useful, limited job.
Read first
Limit observation tools to the demo namespace. Do not expose credentials, Secrets, arbitrary shell access, or unrestricted cluster writes.
Review the change
The agent may prepare a manifest patch and a PR. Permission checks live in code; a prompt alone does not enforce the boundary.
Stop when uncertain
If evidence is missing, tool limits are reached, or recovery checks fail, report the remaining uncertainty and hand off to the operator.
What happens if the proposed fix makes things worse?
Mark the incident unresolved, preserve the failed checks, and propose a Git revert for review. With Argo CD automated sync, recovery should follow a corrective Git change; its direct rollback operation is unavailable while automated sync is enabled. Read the Argo CD behavior.
How do we handle malicious text in logs?
Treat logs and retrieved documents as untrusted observations. They cannot grant permissions or change the workflow. Validate every tool request against an allowlist, redact sensitive fields, cap output, and require evidence references for proposed changes.
Does OOMKilled always mean “increase memory”?
No. Investigate the workload, recent changes, memory trend, and node pressure. A low limit is one explanation; a leak or an unexpected workload may require a different fix. The example uses a known limit regression so its proposed change can be tested. Read Kubernetes resource guidance.


    
Build the portfolio version
Prove one loop before expanding it.
Recommended scope: one app, three controlled failure classes, and repeatable evaluations.
  1. 01
    Create the incident lab
    Deploy the app, add a health endpoint and metrics, and write reproducible fault injection and reset scripts.
    Done when: all three faults can be reproduced and cleared manually.
  2. 02
    Build the investigator
    Receive an alert, inspect scoped observations, maintain hypotheses, and produce a diagnosis with evidence references.
    Done when: it diagnoses baseline cases and admits missing evidence.
  3. 03
    Complete the change loop
    Generate a validated manifest patch, open a PR, pause for approval, then observe the deployment and health checks.
    Done when: one incident reaches verified recovery end to end.
  4. 04
    Evaluate and explain
    Repeat incidents with variations and distractions. Publish the method, results, failures, architecture, and a short recorded demo.
    Done when: another developer can reproduce the demo and evaluation.
Later, if the evidence supports it
Specialist agents, approved automatic fixes for narrow cases, incident memory, and additional services. Keep them out of the first release.


    
The portfolio differentiator
Measure the agent, not just the demo.
Existing tools already investigate incidents. Your contribution is a reproducible workflow with clear outcome measurements.
MeasureHow to evaluate it
Diagnosis accuracyCompare the supported diagnosis against the injected fault; track wrong answers and abstentions separately.
Recovery successCheck actual requests and health over a defined observation window, not just whether deployment finished.
Unnecessary changesInclude healthy and ambiguous cases; record whether the agent proposes a change without sufficient evidence.
Time and costTrack alert-to-proposal time, recovery time, tool calls, tokens, and model cost per incident.
Boundary complianceTest out-of-scope requests and instructions embedded in logs; confirm forbidden actions are blocked.
No benchmark results exist yet. These are proposed evaluation criteria. Set targets after measuring a first baseline.
